en: Preface to the Compiled Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
The *prajñā* of the self-nature of all sentient beings is equal to that of all Buddhas; it is only because sentient beings have not yet relinquished their deluded attachments.
Therefore, they scatter and rush into the six realms of existence, willingly sinking into them without returning.

For their sake, the World-Honored One has expounded all the *sūtras*, none of which do anything other than cause one to realize, within one's own person, such matters as these that are inherently present.
Yet, while the various *sūtras* differ in their expositions—some being circuitous and some direct, some pure and some mixed—it is only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* [that is otherwise].
This single sutra shatters attachments and severs doubts; it is the most direct and pure teaching. Taken as a whole, it is one; analyzed, it has three aspects:
first, the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), which is like the hardness of gold—this is the sutra of principle (*li*).
Second, the *prajñā* of contemplative observation, which is like the sharpness of gold—this is the sutra of practice (*xing*). Third, the *prajñā* of words and letters... [as in the original text].
The radiance of gold refers to the sutras and treatises of the teachings. Those of sharp faculties attain them perfectly, while those of dull faculties cling to them superficially.

In the past, when the Great Master Huineng heard a guest reciting, "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere," and the Elder Zhongfeng read until he reached, "Shouldering the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Tathāgata," they both attained sudden enlightenment and entry into realization. This is the immediate vision of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
These are the most superior and sharp faculties. Next are those who clearly practice contemplative observation. Below them are those who rely on faith in the written words.

As for those whose faculties consist merely of faith in the written words, these are the lowest. Nevertheless, in this degenerate age, those who enter [the path] suddenly are few; therefore, realization must proceed from principle through practice.
Since practice relies on the teachings for illumination, written words are indeed the ferry and raft for the two kinds of *prajñā*.
Although the text of this sūtra is extremely concise, its meaning encompasses that of the extensive treatises. For those who have entered the higher stages, it is difficult to fathom at first glance;

yet, since the time of its initial translation, there have been approximately several hundred commentaries produced here in this land. Even a shallow interpretation of a profound scripture is said to offer some benefit, let alone one that is partial.
Is there anything in these speculative interpretations that one would find unbearable to hear or see?

Formerly, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga of the Western Regions entered the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* (Sunlight Samādhi) and ascended to Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya regarding the meaning of this sutra.
Maitreya versified it in eighty verses. Upon emerging from samādhi, Asaṅga and his younger brother Vasubandhu each received these verses and composed treatises based upon them. These two...
The mutual explanations in these treatises render the intent of the sutras ever more profound; they remain beyond the comprehension of those with shallow intelligence.

The Great Master of Mount Gui during the Tang dynasty, possessing a nature of wondrous awakening, swam through the ocean of the teachings. Out of compassion for sentient beings, he took the two original treatises as his foundation and extensively gathered various other expositions.

The *Shuchanyao shu* (Commentary on the Essential Explanations) in two fascicles is characterized by its refined diction and ultimate principles; it is the most excellent among all commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
However, those who fail to understand it upon a single reading are still six or seven out of ten. Master Shibi subsequently provided an extensive commentary, yet this was lost in excessive prolixity.

Master Changshui arose again to prune and edit it, producing the *Kanding ji* (Record of the Determined Text), whereby the meaning of the commentary became manifest. Once the meaning of the commentary was made manifest...

Thereafter, the three aspects of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*—its teaching, its practice, and its principle—will be revealed without exception. However, at present, erroneous interpretations abound throughout the world.

Furthermore, the masters who transmit and lecture upon it constantly rely on worldly versions; each remains confined by their own views. For this reason, few truly know how to honor and follow the true tradition. Alas!
Do they not reflect that the gap between the holy and the ordinary, the wise and the ignorant, is as vast as that between clouds and mud? Only Asaṅga has ascended [to the heights].

Asanga was a Bodhisattva on the [ten] stages, while Vasubandhu was a Bodhisattva in the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) prior to the stages; both received the teachings directly from Maitreya.

Maitreya, in turn, was a Great Being in his final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) who received the teachings directly from the World-Honored One Śākyamuni. Since this commentary relies entirely upon these two treatises, the commentary itself is the word of the Buddha.

If the Buddha’s words are not taken as the fundamental authority, whom else could one possibly take as authority? In the past, while perusing the Tripiṭaka, I was fortunate enough to encounter this text.

I studied it with meticulous care and repeated it three times, feeling as though I had obtained a precious treasure. However, because the commentaries and records were circulated separately, it was difficult to investigate them;

the prose and meanings were continuous, and the topical outlines were interspersed, such that even the author himself seemed confused about the structural flow from beginning to end. Thereupon, disregarding my own mediocrity and folly, I took up the brush to [compose this work].
Regarding this matter: I have collated the sutras and commentaries, harmonized the records, and organized the topical divisions.

I have meticulously transcribed and scrutinized the text until three drafts were completed, during which time I carefully revised and refined it to ensure that readers would not suffer from mental confusion or visual dizziness, but rather gain the benefit of resolving their doubts and dispelling their attachments.
I have specially commissioned the carving of woodblocks to facilitate its wide circulation. Some may say: "You are a Chan practitioner; how is it that you..."
"Is this the study of the *Śāstra* commentaries on the *Sūtra*? I replied, "Alas, you have gone too far. Let us not speak of distant matters; consider even the two masters Guishan and Changshui.
One followed the lineage of Dajian (Huineng) and penetrated the source of Chan; the other called upon Langya and awakened to the essential point of the mind.

Both likewise continued the true transmission within the teachings, pointing directly through the very texts themselves. If one possesses the correct eye, how could [this be considered a contradiction]?"

Even those who maintain these two views [of existence and non-existence]—how much more so this Prajñā? It is but another name for the essence of awakening and a distinct title for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*).

Its nature is emptiness, and its conditions are met; by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is without differentiation. The merit of generating the bodhicitta is fundamentally limitless and without boundary.
I shall circulate such a sutra as this, in order to seek the simultaneous benefit of both myself and others. To circulate the written text is to adorn the *nirmāṇakāya*. To circulate...
Penetrating observation and illumination serve to adorn the *saṃbhogakāya*; the circulation of the true mark (*dharmatā*) serves to adorn the *dharmakāya*.

In this way, one becomes fully endowed with the Buddha-body. Why is this? Because the two causes—arising and realization—will certainly bring about accomplishment. As the Sūtra says: "The meaning of this sūtra is inconceivable;
its karmic fruition is also inconceivable. Those who possess merit and wisdom should act in this manner.
Contemplation.
Written on an auspicious day in the middle summer of the Jiachen year of the Kangxi era by the junior disciple Xingce of Jingxi at the Hermitage on the Riverbank in Wulin.

(2) First, the sequential explanation (therefore, it is discussed): [The text continues: "If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, how can one understand the profound Dharma? If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will fall into the views of the heterodox paths. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to escape from the three realms. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to transcend the world. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to benefit sentient beings. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to purify the Buddha-lands. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to fulfill the vows of a Bodhisattva. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to realize the ultimate reality. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to enter the stage of non-retrogression. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to manifest the various transformations. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to comprehend the power of the Tathāgata. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to sever the bonds of ignorance. If one does not know the meaning of the Great Vehicle, one will not be able to attain the wisdom of omniscience. [The text continues: "Therefore, one must first understand the meaning of the Great Vehicle. What is the meaning of the Great Vehicle?

It is the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of signlessness, the meaning of wishlessness, the meaning of non-arising, the meaning of non-ceasing, the meaning of non-birth, the meaning of non-death, the meaning of non-coming, the meaning of non-going, the meaning of non-existence, the meaning of non-non-existence, the meaning of neither existence nor non-existence, the meaning of the Middle Way, the meaning of the Dharma-realm, the meaning of the nature of phenomena, the meaning of suchness, the meaning of the limit of reality, the meaning of the unconditioned, the meaning of the ungraspable, the meaning of the ineffable, the meaning of the inconceivable, the meaning of the peerless, the meaning of the incomparable, the meaning of the unsurpassed, the meaning of the unexcelled, the meaning of the ultimate, the meaning of the absolute, the meaning of the true, the meaning of the real, the meaning of the eternal, the meaning of the blissful, the meaning of the self, and the meaning of the pure. This is called the meaning of the Great Vehicle. [The text continues: "By knowing this meaning, one can then understand all the teachings of the Buddha. By understanding these teachings, one can then practice the path. By practicing the path, one can then sever all afflictions. By severing all afflictions, one can then attain liberation. By attaining liberation, one can then benefit sentient beings. By benefiting sentient beings, one can then purify the Buddha-lands. By purifying the Buddha-lands, one can then fulfill the vows of a Bodhisattva. By fulfilling the vows of a Bodhisattva, one can then realize the ultimate reality. By realizing the ultimate reality, one can then enter the stage of non-retrogression. By entering the stage of non-retrogression, one can then manifest the various transformations. By manifesting the various transformations, one can then comprehend the power of the Tathāgata. By comprehending the power of the Tathāgata, one can then sever the bonds of ignorance. By severing the bonds of ignorance, one can then attain the wisdom of omniscience. Therefore, one should diligently study and contemplate the meaning of the Great Vehicle."

Diagram of the Eighteen Stages of Abiding.
Explanation of the Diagram of the Eighteen Stages of Abiding (18-zhu-jie-wei-tu):

The first stage of abiding corresponds to the Stage of Initial Aspiration (*prathama-cittotpāda*), and it subsumes the preceding ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) as well as the remaining nine stages of abiding; together, these constitute twenty mental states.
The second stage consists of the six *pāramitās*; therefore, it is subsequently assigned to the six practices. The fourth stage comprises the factors of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya-aṅga*).

Regarding the realization through verbal expression, within that realization, the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and merit (*puṇya-lakṣaṇa*) are distinguished; therefore, these are assigned to the final three practices.

In the eighteenth [chapter], there are six kinds of fulfillment (*paripūri*): the first fulfillment is assigned to the ten stages from the second bhūmi up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);
the latter five unsurpassed fulfillments are assigned to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*pranidhāna-bodhi*). The remaining assignments may be seen accordingly.
To examine in detail the stages taught in the various teachings, they differ in their gradations. Some speak of fifty-two stages;

others subsume the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) within the ten abidings (*vihāra*), thus speaking of only forty-two stages. Within these, some further expand the former while condensing the latter.
The latter opens up what was closed before; sometimes both the former and the latter are opened together, or both are closed together.

When opened, it is broad; when closed, it is narrow. Furthermore, there are those who use the small to illustrate the great, or the provisional to illustrate the real. Regarding names, positions, and designations, their transitions and entries are confusing and erroneous. By following the names while neglecting the essential intent, many errors are seen.
This even extends to the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other scriptures, which vanish entirely [from their understanding]; while the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda* and other sūtras remain complete.
To speak of existence, non-existence, breadth, or narrowness—all such teachings are expounded according to what is appropriate.

Only in the *Avataṃsaka* are the myriad distinctions of sequential practice (*paṅpu*) and the single limit of perfect fusion (*yuanrong*) both present; where existence, non-existence, breadth, and narrowness are entirely without obstruction, only then is it the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Why is this so? Because from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*), there is non-existence; from the perspective of persons (*pudgala*), there is existence. As the present sutra says: "All worthies..."
The Sages all possess distinctions by means of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Because they are unconditioned, they are non-existent; because they possess distinctions, they exist.

Within these distinctions, there is no lack of variation in breadth and narrowness. Since the Master [Vasubandhu] reveres his Teacher [Maitreya], who occupies the seat of succession, he thoroughly understands the meaning of the sūtras.

Because he clarifies both the doctrinal schools and the principles, he correctly abides in the Middle Way, falling neither into existence nor non-existence. Since he manifests both the Dharma and its analogies equally, from beginning to end—
In the interim, having measured the breadth and narrowness [of the stages], the eighteen abodes were assigned and the three grounds and five positions were explained;

this is truly exhaustive and excellent. The Master of the Commentary (*Ji-zhu*) said: "However, the practitioner must, in every thought-moment, merge with the Buddha-realm and trace back to the ultimate ocean of fruition.

It is naturally so that the successive stages differ. If one pre-emptively applies the mind according to fixed grades, it will ultimately obstruct entry into realization. Moreover, the essence of this sutra has no..."

As for the marks (*lakṣaṇa*), how could they possibly be arranged according to the depth or shallowness of one's rank? Rather, as emotional delusions gradually thin out and one’s stage (*bhūmi*) rises higher, their essential characteristics become somewhat similar;
thus, they are briefly correlated and subsumed. This statement is correct. Yet, people today have those who take offense at this on account of Asaṅga. Alas!
Failing to understand that one must realize the marks while remaining detached from the marks, they falsely claim that there is exclusively no-mark (*animitta*). Consequently, they fall [into error].
Arrogance leads to a failure to distinguish between cause and effect, resulting in the erroneous adherence to scriptural tenets and the slander of former sages.

May those who sincerely study Prajñāpāramitā take care not to follow such one-sided views. Abiding in the Middle Way, leaving behind hindrances to realize the truth, and relying on unconditioned dharmas to enter the ranks of the noble ones—then one may hope to be free from error.
The Twenty-Seven Diagrams of the Interconnected Veins of Doubt.

Regarding the first diagram, titled "The Principal," it refers to giving without dwelling upon signs (*animitta-dāna*). Because this constitutes the principal object of doubt, it is treated sequentially.
It begins and extends to the twenty-seventh [chapter]. Among these, the third chapter presents ten doubts, and the eleventh generally summarizes the preceding doubts;
this constitutes the core structural juncture. The remaining doubts can be understood accordingly.
The Buddha is an inconceivable person; the sutra is called the "Inconceivable Teaching. As for "inconceivable," it cannot be understood through conceptual thought.
That which cannot be understood through conceptual thought can only be understood by one who is free from conceptual thought.

That which can be understood by one free from conceptual thought is ultimately such that it cannot be understood by conceptual thought at all. Why is this? Because the twenty-seven doubts mentioned above have arisen.

Apart from the scriptural text itself, these matters already transcend the reach of thought. Nevertheless, there are those that arrive in sequential order, those that arrive by skipping over [intervals], those that arrive through comprehensive penetration, and those that arrive by being received in parts.
In such cases, the sequence may be understood; however, when there is a skip, it is difficult to comprehend.
How much more so when it is universally pervasive and inherited through distinct lineages? It is like the blood vessels within the body or the spring currents beneath the earth;
their channels and branches lie hidden and flow silently, which is by no means an ordinary matter. This is comparable to those who find it easy to understand the principles manifested in the texts.

How much less can one who employs a coarse or superficial mind, following their own preconceptions to engage in reckless fabrication, have anything to do with the meaning of the scriptures? Therefore, it is said:

It cannot be understood through ordinary thought. Maitreya, with the wisdom of one in the position of succession, harmonized this sutra of subtle awakening and expounded these inconceivable verses for those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*), saying:
"To sever various doubts. Vasubandhu first unraveled the thread of doubt and wove it throughout the sutra, saying:
"To sever twenty-seven kinds of doubt. Therefore, it is said: "Only those beyond the reach of thought can understand it. Formerly...

Those who seek the meaning through the literal text encounter so many contradictions. Now, by determining the text through its underlying structure (*mài*), the conflict between the stars Sirius and Procyon is resolved.
What appeared as deviation is seen as conformity; what was blocked is seen as penetration; what was severed is seen as continuity; what was obscure is seen as clarity.

This subtle and profound insight—the power of one who is empty of preconceptions, honors antiquity, and seeks with diligence—is why it is said: "Unless one reaches the ultimate beyond conceptual thought, [the truth] cannot be realized."
One is able to understand it. Those with a sincere mind who study the Prajñāpāramitā should clarify their spirits and collect their thoughts, studying it thoroughly and examining it minutely.
Then, the entire body and vital pulse of this sutra will leap forth clearly beyond the surface of its words, phrases, and verses.

Thereby, one will forever sever all doubts, deeply comprehend its meaning and intent, and give rise to practice based on that understanding; as practice arises, understanding is transcended, such that there is no hindrance to proceeding from [understanding]...
To personally arrive at the realm beyond thought within the midst of thought is to personally behold the inconceivable person and personally hear the inconceivable teaching.
One must still strive toward this!
Preface:
This sutra has been translated six times; the version from the Qin dynasty is considered the most excellent. As its dissemination became widespread, errors and corruptions increased considerably.

Consequently, even when comparing various annotated editions, discrepancies and contradictions abound. The characters and phrases of the present edition have been verified and corrected strictly according to the original text of the Northern Canon.
There are approximately several hundred commentaries on this sutra. Although there are several authoritative sub-commentaries, each possesses its own strengths and weaknesses.

That which is perfectly excellent and beautiful is found in the *Zuanyao* (Essential Compendium) alone. Therefore, the text of the present commentary follows the original entirely, with no daring alterations.
As for the *Kanding ji* (Record of Collation and Determination), it has already been integrated into the main commentary below, at its beginning.
There is no opening or closing [of the text], nor is there any addition or subtraction of characters; the aim is simply to ensure that the phrasing and meaning are appropriate.

Generally, in combined editions of commentaries (*shu*) and sub-commentaries (*chao*), it is common to see both texts written side-by-side, with the heading "Commentary and Sub-commentary" placed at the beginning.
There are two inconveniences: first, when encountering passages that are analyzed in meticulous detail, the marking characters become overly cumbersome;
second, the meaning is not yet settled. This is because a sub-commentary (*chao*) cannot be ranked alongside a commentary (*shu*), just as a commentary cannot be equated with the scripture (*jing*).
For example, the scripture is the father, the commentary is the son, and the sub-commentary is the grandson. Such is the natural order of their relationship.
There ought to be a distinction. In the current first two fascicles, the commentary (*śāstra*) text is written flush left, while the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) is indented by one character.

From the third fascicle onward, however, the sūtra text is written flush left, the commentary is indented by one character from the sūtra, and the sub-commentary is further indented by one character from the commentary—this differing from the format of other editions.
Furthermore, within the sub-commentary, there are passages explaining the sūtra that do not yet involve the commentary.
It is my intention that these be placed before the commentary so as not to disrupt the sequential order.
Within this section, one must distinguish four different types of topical outlines (*pīn-ti*): the outline of the commentary listed within the sub-commentary;
the outline of the sūtra listed within the commentary; and the outline of the commentary itself listed within the commentary, along with its sectional exegesis.
The sections of the sutra are layered, repetitive, and disordered, causing much confusion for beginners. Now, the first two types have all been distinguished by the addition of circles;
furthermore, they are rendered in black and white so that the structural lineage from beginning to end may flow through the commentary and notes.
As for the latter two types, they shall be transcribed according to the standard format of the commentary, so that they may be clearly and orderly perceived.
Regarding the topical outlines (*kō*) within the *Jì* (Commentary): where there were omissions that left what precedes incomplete or what follows deficient, I have ventured to supplement them.
Where there were outlines that ought to be established but were not, I have added them. Where the *Shū* (Sub-commentary) lists an outline and the *Jì* lists it again, I have pruned the redundancy.

Where headings were placed for convenience at the expense of the proper sequence, I have rearranged them according to their correct positions. And where the names of the sections were not entirely optimal, I have briefly revised them.
These figures are not presented out of mere audacity or arbitrary preference, but with the sincere aim of ensuring accuracy. May readers not harbor doubts regarding discrepancies or omissions.

Between the eighteen and nineteen characters of the nineteenth fascicle, there is a passage from "At that time, the Venerable Subhūti" to "this is called a sentient being," totaling sixty-two characters.
This was originally absent from the Qin translation and was added by later generations.
It is included [in the root text], and thus the commentary does not explain it. However, it exists in the Wei translation, and both treatises also explain it;
there is no fault in adding it. Moreover, since the *Jì* (Commentary) contains supplementary explanations, I have now added it following the worldly version.
This is just as in the "Universal Gateway" chapter of the Qin translation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, where the verses from the Sui period were added without any fault.

The allocation of the eighteen abodes (*vihāra*) and the severance of the twenty-seven doubts constitute the fundamental principles of the two treatises and the pivotal essentials of the single scripture.

If the stages of realization (*bhūmi*) are not clarified, one will remain ignorant of the horizontal classification; if the structural connections are not made clear, one will be confused regarding the vertical exposition.
Therefore, I have now prepared diagrams and explanations for each, appended to the end of the entire work, so that upon opening the volume and consulting the diagrams, one may see clearly.
However, as these [passages] are present before our eyes, they do not require consulting other texts to resolve their difficulties.

Yet, within both the *Śāstra* (commentary) and the *Vivaraṇa* (sub-commentary), there are numerous errors in both characters and phrasing. Since even the Northern Canon cannot be relied upon, what need is there to mention other editions?
Now, therefore, I have weighed the textual meaning; if even a single character was not in its proper place, I have searched for it exhaustively.

I obtained this from an old manuscript. At times, through deep reflection, I attained personal realization and was relieved of all doubt. I have carefully extracted various errors and appended them to the end of this volume.
This serves both to demonstrate the difficulty of collation and to expose the mistakes in the Tripitaka edition.
May the readers take full note of this.
